title: Der Fuchs und die Gänse
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 86. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (fieng).
about: The eighty-sixth tale (KHM 86), and one of the shortest and driest in the collection: a fox corners a flock of geese in a meadow and, before he will eat them, allows the condemned one last request — a prayer. The joke is that the prayer never has to end, and the tale lets it run exactly as long as the geese need it to.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs kam einmal auf eine Wiese, wo eine Herde schöner fetter Gänse saß, da lachte er und sprach „ich komme ja wie gerufen, ihr sitzt hübsch beisammen, so kann ich eine nach der andern auffressen.“
sentences.l: The fox came once upon a meadow, where a flock of fine fat geese sat, then he laughed and said “I come just as if called, you sit prettily together, so I can eat up one after the other.”
sentences.i: The fox came one day into a meadow where a flock of fine fat geese was sitting, and he laughed and said, “I come as though I had been sent for; you are sitting nicely together, so I can eat you up one after another.”
sentences.n: eine Herde is a flock or a herd — a different word from der Herd, a hearth, which is what the shared glossary answers this spelling with elsewhere; the entry is corrected for this tale. schöner fetter Gänse is a genitive plural after Herde, “of fine fat geese”, and saß stays singular because the collective Herde is the subject. wie gerufen, “as if called”, is a set phrase for arriving just at the right moment. sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen where modern German would have sagte.

sentences.t: Die Gänse gackerten vor Schrecken, sprangen auf, fiengen an zu jammern und kläglich um ihr Leben zu bitten.
sentences.l: The geese cackled from fright, sprang up, began to wail and pitifully to beg for their life.
sentences.i: The geese cackled with fright, sprang up, and fell to wailing and pleading pitifully for their lives.
sentences.n: vor before a feeling names its cause: vor Schrecken, “from fright”. fiengen an is the 1857 spelling of fingen an, from separable anfangen; the particle an stands at the end of its clause and the two zu-infinitives that follow both hang from it. um etwas bitten is to beg for something. Leben is singular in the German, one life shared among them all.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs aber wollte auf nichts hören und sprach „da ist keine Gnade, ihr müßt sterben.“
sentences.l: The fox however would listen to nothing and said “there is no mercy, you must die.”
sentences.i: But the fox would hear of nothing, and said, “There is no mercy here; you must die.”
sentences.n: auf etwas hören is to listen to something, to heed it — more than plain hören, to hear. müßt is the 1857 spelling of müsst, the plural “you must”; the shared entry describes a different, subjunctive use of this spelling and is corrected for this tale. da is the loose “there” of a situation rather than a place.

sentences.t: Endlich nahm sich eine das Herz und sagte „sollen wir armen Gänse doch einmal unser jung frisch Leben lassen, so erzeige uns die einzige Gnade und erlaub uns noch ein Gebet, damit wir nicht in unsern Sünden sterben:
sentences.l: At last one took herself the heart and said “if we poor geese are indeed to leave our young fresh life, then show us the one mercy and allow us one more prayer, so that we do not die in our sins:
sentences.i: At last one of them took heart and said, “If we poor geese must give up our young fresh lives after all, then grant us this one mercy and allow us one prayer more, so that we do not die in our sins;
sentences.n: sich das Herz nehmen, “to take oneself the heart”, is to summon the courage. sollen wir … lassen with the verb first is a conditional without wenn: “if we are to …”; the so that follows means “then”. das Leben lassen is to lose or give up one’s life. jung frisch stands uninflected before Leben, an old freedom the 1857 text keeps. erzeige and erlaub are imperatives to the fox.

sentences.t: hernach wollen wir uns auch in eine Reihe stellen, damit du dir immer die fetteste aussuchen kannst.“
sentences.l: afterward we will also place ourselves in a row, so that you can always pick out for yourself the fattest.”
sentences.i: afterwards we will set ourselves in a row too, so that you may always choose the fattest for yourself.”
sentences.n: hernach is an older word for afterwards. sich stellen is to place oneself; dir is a dative of interest, and sich etwas aussuchen is to pick something out for oneself. die fetteste is the superlative of fett with the noun Gans left unsaid.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der Fuchs, „das ist billig, und ist eine fromme Bitte: betet, ich will so lange warten.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the fox, “that is fair, and is a pious request: pray, I will wait that long.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the fox, “that is only fair, and it is a pious request. Pray, then; I will wait so long.”
sentences.n: billig here carries its older sense, fair and reasonable, not cheap. und ist has no subject — German may drop es in the second half of such a pair. Bitte is the noun, a request; the shared glossary answers this spelling with the verb bitten, so the entry is corrected here. betet is the imperative to more than one.

sentences.t: Also fieng die erste ein recht langes Gebet an, immer „ga! ga!“
sentences.l: So the first began a good long prayer, always “ga! ga!”
sentences.i: So the first set up a right long prayer, on and on, “ga! ga!”
sentences.n: fieng … an is separable anfangen with the particle waiting at the end of the clause; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. recht before an adjective is “good and”, quite. ga! ga! is the goose’s honking, not a word — the shared glossary answers this spelling with a Low German imperative meaning “go”, which belongs to other tales, and the entry is corrected here.

sentences.t: und weil sie gar nicht aufhören wollte, wartete die zweite nicht, bis die Reihe an sie kam, sondern fieng auch an „ga! ga!“
sentences.l: and because she would not stop at all, the second did not wait until the turn came to her, but began too “ga! ga!”
sentences.i: and because she would not leave off at all, the second did not wait for her turn to come, but began as well, “ga! ga!”
sentences.n: gar nicht is “not at all”. die Reihe kommt an jemanden — the turn comes round to someone; Reihe is the same word the goose used for the row they promised to form, and the tale lets the two senses lean on each other. sondern is the “but” that must follow a negative.

sentences.t: Die dritte und vierte folgte ihr, und bald gackerten sie alle zusammen.
sentences.l: The third and fourth followed her, and soon they all cackled together.
sentences.i: The third and the fourth followed her, and soon they were all cackling together.
sentences.n: folgte is singular although two subjects stand before it — the 1857 text takes them as one. folgen governs the dative, so ihr is “her”, not “to her” in English.

sentences.t: (Und wenn sie ausgebetet haben, soll das Märchen weiter erzählt werden, sie beten aber alleweile noch immer fort.)
sentences.l: (And when they have prayed out, the tale shall be told further, but they are praying meanwhile still on and on.)
sentences.i: (And when they have finished praying, the tale shall be told on — but they are at their prayers to this hour, and have not stopped yet.)
sentences.n: The round brackets are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text. ausbeten is built like austrinken or ausreden: the aus- marks the praying through to the end. In the last clause fortbeten, to go on praying, is separable, and its fort comes to rest at the very end. alleweile is an old word for all this while. The tale ends on the joke that it cannot go on, because the prayer never finishes.

glossary.bitte: die Bitte — request, plea (nom./acc. sg.; also bitte: I ask, from bitten)
glossary.ga: ga! — the goose’s honk, not a word (in this tale the geese’s cry; elsewhere ga is Low German for geh, go)
glossary.herde: die Herde — herd, flock (nom. sg.; not der Herd, hearth)
glossary.lassen: lassen — to leave, give up (here das Leben lassen: to lose one’s life); also: to let, to have something done
glossary.müßt: müssen — must (2nd pl. present; 1857 spelling of müsst)
